strengths: Introduces and formalizes a new and practically relevant task: distractor-free generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, combining feedforward cross-scene 3DGS with distractor masking.

Proposes a coherent training paradigm with reference-based mask prediction, mask refinement, and auxiliary reference-view supervision to improve mask accuracy and training stability under distractors.
Proposes a two-stage inference framework with reference scoring and distractor pruning to select cleaner references and reduce residual distractor artifacts in rendered novel views.

Extensive experiments across real RobustNeRF and On-the-go data plus synthetic Re10K/ACID scenes, with comparisons to re-trained, pre-trained, and fine-tuned baselines, component ablations, and analyses of K, N, and reference scoring.

Quantitative results show substantial improvements over re-trained generalizable 3DGS baselines under distractor data and competitive or better mask prediction compared with a scene-specific distractor-free method.
The potential to combine with existing generalizable 3DGS frameworks and the promise to release code/models supports reproducibility and future adoption.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely incremental: the work combines existing components from distractor-free reconstruction (robust masks, entity segmentation, reference warping, reference scoring/pruning) into a generalizable 3DGS pipeline, without a fundamentally new architecture, learning algorithm, or theoretical insight.

Several technical formulations are unclear or potentially incorrect. In particular, Eq. 7 defines a disparity-induced error mask as the union of warped one-filled reference masks, but this union represents target regions visible in at least one reference, not regions absent from all references as claimed; this discrepancy needs clarification and may affect the method.

The evaluation is limited: only a few real scenes/datasets are used, no statistical significance or error bars are reported, and the synthetic distractor data is constructed by inserting COCO objects, which may not capture realistic in-the-wild distractor complexity.

The method depends heavily on a pre-trained entity segmentation model; segmentation failures can propagate through mask prediction, reference scoring, and pruning, and the robustness of this dependency is not thoroughly evaluated.
Distractor pruning can create holes or speckle artifacts when distractor regions overlap with commonly occluded areas; the paper acknowledges this limitation but does not fully solve it.

Efficiency and reproducibility are only partially addressed: the two-stage inference and segmentation add overhead, code/models are not yet available, and important implementation details and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses appear relegated to an appendix.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and relatively unexplored task: distractor-free generalizable 3DGS, combining feedforward 3DGS with distractor handling.
Introduces a reference-based mask prediction idea that uses re-rendered reference consistency to correct robust-loss masks, which is intuitive and potentially useful.
Proposes a two-stage inference framework with reference scoring and distractor pruning; components are reasonable and ablation studies show incremental gains.
Reports experiments on real (On-the-go, RobustNeRF) and synthetic (Re10K/ACID with COCO distractors) datasets, with comparisons to several generalizable and distractor-free baselines.
Quantitative results show consistent improvements over MVSplat and adapted masking baselines on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, and ablations support the contribution of each component.
Efficiency is comparable to the baseline when segmentation is cached; code and models are promised.
weaknesses: The central claim that generalizable mask prediction outperforms scene-specific methods is not quantitatively supported. The paper provides only qualitative mask visualizations (Fig. 6) and no mask IoU/accuracy metrics against ground-truth masks.

Evaluation protocol is ambiguous regarding distractor-containing query views: it is unclear whether PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS are computed after masking distractor pixels in the ground truth. If not, metrics would unfairly penalize distractor-free reconstructions.

Several equations are technically unclear or appear inconsistent. For example, Eq. 6 unions the filtered mask with M_Rob, which cannot remove false-positive distractor labels from M_Rob; Eq. 7 defines M_D as a union of warped one-filled reference masks, which represents regions visible in at least one reference rather than regions absent from all references, so the disparity-error mask appears mis-specified.

The novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing robust-loss masking, pre-trained entity segmentation, warping/filtering, and two-stage inference. The core reference-based filtering is intuitive but not a fundamentally new technical insight.

Reference Scoring depends on coarse 3DGS and masks from initially sampled references; if those initial references are distractor-heavy, scoring may be unreliable and circular. The use of mask pixel count as a proxy for both distractor level and disparity is hand-wavy and not validated.

Distractor Pruning may create holes or speckle artifacts, and the paper only avoids pruning common occlusions. There is no quantitative analysis of hole/artifact reduction, nor a user study or perceptual metric beyond LPIPS.
The synthetic experiments are only qualitatively shown in Fig. 10, despite being used to support the method; no quantitative synthetic results are provided in the main paper.

Important implementation details are missing from the main text (training iterations, optimizer, batch size, hardware, scene splits, segmentation model specifics, threshold sensitivity), limiting reproducibility without the appendix.

Baseline comparisons may be unfavorable to scene-specific distractor-free methods, which are adapted to a cross-scene generalizable setting and are not designed for it; some require Colmap/Nerfacto or per-scene hyperparameters unavailable in this setting.
No oracle-mask or per-scene optimized upper-bound comparison is provided, so it is difficult to isolate how much gain comes from better masking versus generalizable training.

The claim of 'without any mask supervision' is misleading, since the method relies on a pre-trained Entity Segmentation model and robust-loss heuristics, which involve external supervision and assumptions.
The writing is rough and often hard to follow, with inconsistent terminology, missing punctuation, and confusing equation/figure references (e.g., 'Eq. 4678', 'Fig.3 6').

strengths: Addresses a novel and practical problem: distractor-free generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, with the first formulation of this cross-scene feedforward setting.

The training paradigm is well motivated and technically sound, combining reference-based mask prediction, mask decoupling/refinement, entity segmentation, and an auxiliary reference loss to improve distractor masking under cross-scene training.
The two-stage inference framework with reference scoring and distractor pruning is a sensible approach for reducing artifacts/holes caused by residual distractors and limited references.

Extensive experiments on real (RobustNeRF, On-the-go) and synthetic (Re10K, ACID with inserted distractors) datasets compare against retrained generalizable 3DGS methods and adapted scene-specific distractor-free methods.
Ablations clearly validate the contribution of each training and inference component, including the reference scoring mechanism and distractor pruning.

Results show substantial quantitative improvements, e.g., DGGS achieving 21.74 PSNR on the five-scene mean versus 15.45 for the MVSplat baseline and 19.29 for the best adapted scene-specific masking baseline.
The method is designed to integrate with existing generalizable 3DGS frameworks such as MVSplat, increasing its potential impact and applicability.
weaknesses: The claim of 'without any mask supervision' is somewhat misleading: the method relies on a pre-trained entity segmentation model and robust-mask heuristics, and it does not fully analyze sensitivity to segmentation failures or domain shift.

Quantitative evaluation of mask quality is limited. The claim that mask prediction is superior to scene-specific methods is mainly supported qualitatively, without mask IoU/accuracy metrics or statistical significance analysis.

The Reference Scoring mechanism is under-explained and potentially ambiguous: Eq. 10 uses pixel-wise mask summation for selection, but it is not fully clear how this simultaneously balances distractor size, disparity, and view coverage.

Distractor Pruning is heuristic and conditionally applied to avoid common occlusions; it can still produce speckle artifacts when references share occluded regions, as acknowledged in the limitations.

Key implementation details are missing from the main manuscript, including network architecture, loss weights, segmentation model specifics, synthetic data generation protocol, and exact composition of the five-scene mean; the appendix is not available in the provided manuscript.

Efficiency is degraded by the two-stage inference and segmentation steps (0.148s vs. 0.084s for MVSplat), and the proposed mitigation via lower resolution or lighter segmentation is not quantitatively evaluated.

Some technical aspects need clarification: Eq. 6 unions the reference-based mask with the robust mask, which may preserve distractor false positives if the robust mask incorrectly marks them as non-distractor; the rationale deserves more analysis.

While comparisons to adapted scene-specific distractor-free methods are useful, fairness of retraining these baselines in the generalizable cross-scene setting is not fully detailed, especially regarding hyperparameter tuning and scene-specific assumptions.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes a novel and practical task, Distractor-free Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, bridging generalizable feed-forward 3DGS and distractor handling in unconstrained captures.

Proposes a coherent framework with a training paradigm (reference-based mask prediction, mask refinement, auxiliary loss) and an inference framework (reference scoring, distractor pruning) that can be integrated into existing generalizable 3DGS pipelines.
Exploits 3D consistency across references to infer distractor masks in a feed-forward manner without mask supervision, which is a sensible and effective idea for the generalizable setting.

Provides extensive experiments on real and synthetic distractor datasets, including comparisons to retrained generalizable baselines and adapted scene-specific distractor-free methods, multiple ablations, efficiency analysis, fine-tuning results, and failure-case discussion.
Reports consistent quantitative and qualitative improvements over strong baselines, demonstrating better training stability and reduced inference artifacts/holes.
weaknesses: The claim that feed-forward mask prediction achieves accuracy superior to scene-specific distractor-free methods is not quantitatively supported by mask accuracy metrics (e.g., IoU); qualitative mask comparisons and downstream reconstruction metrics are insufficient to fully substantiate this central claim.

The method relies on a pre-trained entity segmentation model and caching of its outputs; although ablations show limited impact, this dependence may affect reproducibility and generalization to new domains.

Several design choices are somewhat heuristic and not fully specified in the main text, e.g., exact mask decoupling/recombination logic, distractor pruning criteria, and notation inconsistencies about whether masks encode static or distractor regions.

The comparisons to adapted scene-specific distractor-free methods require nontrivial modifications to fit the generalizable training loop, and it is unclear whether all baselines were optimally tuned under this new setting.
The inference stage requires an extended image pool and multiple forward passes, slightly reducing efficiency, and common occlusions across all references remain a failure mode.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored intersection between distractor-free reconstruction and generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting.
Proposes a modular training and inference framework that can in principle be integrated into existing generalizable 3DGS pipelines.
Uses multi-view 3D consistency and reference re-rendering for mask prediction, which is an intuitive and reasonable direction.
Conducts extensive experiments on real and synthetic datasets, including ablations for training/inference components and efficiency analysis.
Constructs a synthetic distractor dataset and evaluates cross-scene generalization, showing some evidence of robustness.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing components such as robust residual masks, entity segmentation, reference filtering, reference scoring, and primitive pruning, with no major technical breakthrough.

Technical soundness is questionable: Eq. 5 uses a union operation to 'filter' robust masks, and Eq. 6 describes merging one-filled masks via union to find disparity regions, both of which are confusing or potentially incorrect and lack rigorous justification.

The central claim that feed-forward mask prediction achieves accuracy superior to scene-specific distractor-free methods is only shown qualitatively; no quantitative mask IoU/accuracy metrics are provided.

Evaluation fairness is weak: scene-specific distractor-free methods are adapted to the generalizable setting and may be substantially weakened, while comparisons to robust generalizable 3DGS baselines trained with simple robust losses or uncertainty are missing.

Quantitative gains over pretrained Mvsplat* are modest (e.g., 21.74 vs. 20.03 PSNR on five scenes), while very large gains often come from oracle settings such as using distractor-free references during inference.
The synthetic dataset is built by pasting COCO objects into static scenes, which is simplistic and may not reflect real-world distractor complexity.

Efficiency is worse than claimed: the two-stage inference is reported as 0.148s vs. 0.084s for Mvsplat, roughly 1.8x slower, despite being described as a 'slight decrease'; memory/time tradeoffs are not fully explored.
Failure cases such as common occlusions and residual artifacts are acknowledged but not solved; distractor pruning can induce white speckle artifacts.
Clarity and reproducibility are insufficient: several equations and symbols are undefined or confusing, some operations appear inconsistent, and code is not yet available.
Positioning is incomplete: concurrent robust/generalizable 3DGS works are not sufficiently discussed, and there is little analysis of when the reference-based filtering paradigm fails.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes a new and practically relevant task, Distractor-free Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, extending generalizable 3DGS to unconstrained distractor-containing scenes.

Proposes a well-motivated training paradigm with reference-based mask prediction, mask refinement, disparity-error decoupling, and auxiliary supervision, enabling distractor-aware training without mask annotations.

Develops a novel two-stage inference framework with Reference Scoring and Distractor Pruning that selects cleaner references and suppresses residual distractor artifacts in feed-forward novel view synthesis.

Provides extensive experiments on real and synthetically constructed distractor datasets, including comparisons against adapted state-of-the-art distractor-free methods, multiple ablations, efficiency analysis, and cross-scene evaluation.
Reports significant quantitative gains over strong baselines and demonstrates that the learned feed-forward masks can rival scene-specific distractor-free masking qualitatively.
The method is designed to be plug-compatible with existing generalizable 3DGS frameworks, and reproducibility is supported by detailed appendix and a promise to release code.
weaknesses: The central claim about superior distractor mask prediction is supported mainly by qualitative visual comparisons; no quantitative mask quality metrics (e.g., IoU/accuracy against ground-truth masks) are reported, despite synthetic data being available.

Real-world evaluation is limited to a small number of scenes, and the constructed synthetic benchmark is not an established standard; broader evaluation across more diverse datasets would strengthen the claims.

The overall pipeline relies on several existing components, including the RobustNeRF-style initial mask and pre-trained segmentation models; the segmentation module’s contribution is shown to be limited, making the technical novelty partly incremental.
The Reference Scoring mechanism uses heuristics based on predicted mask area and disparity, but its robustness under arbitrary scene-image pools and failure modes is not fully analyzed.

Common occlusions across references and unseen regions remain challenging, and the method does not address generative completion of missing regions; efficiency also degrades due to two-stage inference and segmentation.
